submissions.description: A claim about an AWS API goes in. The smallest read-only call that would settle it goes out, signed and sent to the live API, and the raw response comes back beside the claim. Built after a scan of 119 documented constraints turned out to be measuring the AWS CLI instead of the API.
submissions.markdownDescription:
<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JcnBQm1q7ef1CK1ewbSCxbnvjO/Code.webp?imgSize=1672x941" />

Live: [https://d3c6qhc2pagxm.cloudfront.net](https://d3c6qhc2pagxm.cloudfront.net)

Category: `#workplace-efficiency` · Track: `#community`

Firsthand started as a measurement: how often do the AWS service models disagree with the live AWS API? Partway through, the tool doing the measuring turned out to be one of the things disagreeing. That is the short version of why this exists.

## What it does

You write down something you were told about an AWS API — by the documentation, by a blog post, by your coding agent. Firsthand picks the smallest read-only call that would settle it, runs that call against the real API, and shows you the claim and the raw response side by side.

Write it in whatever language you think in. The claim goes to Bedrock as prose either way, so English and Japanese both produce a working probe, and the list of recent checks carries a machine translation beside anything written in the other language. The original is never rewritten — it is stored exactly as typed, with the translation kept in a separate field and labelled as ours. A claim is evidence of what someone believed, and evidence that has been silently improved is not evidence. The API's response is never translated at all.

Checks are public. What you type is stored and appears in that list.

Then it asks you one question, and only one: have you been bitten by this?

## Where the first measurement went wrong

The first pass was a scan. Pull the constraints out of the botocore service models — the definitions that generate the AWS SDKs, the CLI, and the API reference — then send a value one step past each declared boundary and see whether the API rejects it. Read-only operations only, no required parameters, so nothing gets created and nothing gets touched.

Driven through the AWS CLI, that scan flagged 119 numeric constraints the API did not appear to enforce.

Re-running all 119 as directly signed requests changes the answer. Seventy hold up. Thirty-seven do not, and every single one of those thirty-seven is a parameter named `MaxItems` — the AWS CLI's own client-side paging flag. The CLI consumes `--max-items` and never puts it on the wire, so it will accept any number you hand it, including numbers the API rejects. Not one parameter outside that name was a false positive. The remaining twelve are inconclusive: permissions, unavailable services, request shapes the generic client declines to build.

`acm ListCertificates` is the clean demonstration. Through the CLI, `--max-items 1001` returns successfully. The same value, signed and sent directly:

```
HTTP 400 ValidationException
Value of the input at 'maxItems' failed to satisfy constraint:
Member must have value less than or equal to 1000
```

So the first number was not measuring what it claimed to measure. Four sources describe how AWS behaves — your agent, the docs, the AWS CLI, and the API itself — and the one most people reach for to check is not the API.

A word on the denominators, since they move: 431 services ship a definition file with the AWS CLI, 411 of those speak a wire format this tool handles, and 339 of those actually declare a constraint worth probing. The rest have nothing to check. Split by what they declare, 318 services carry 1,615 numeric bounds and 147 carry 631 enum parameters, with 126 in both groups.

To be clear about proportion: the documentation is overwhelmingly right. Out of those 631 enum parameters, six disagreed with the live API. This is a tool for the exception, not an accusation.

## What the measurement found

Six enum parameters whose declared values and accepted values differ, and seventy declared numeric maximums across twenty-four services that the API does not enforce. Seventy-six differences in total, across twenty-six services. All seventy of the numeric ones are upper bounds; not a single declared minimum survived the re-run. Seventy is a floor rather than a total, because the re-run only covered the cases the CLI had already flagged.

Conditions, since they matter for a number like that: one AWS account, read-only credentials, `ap-northeast-1`, each probe a single request carrying one value one step outside the declared bound. A 200 means the request was accepted, not that a thousand results came back.

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JcoaCAvbhn5pbxyKvEqhA4OL3m/shot.webp?imgSize=1200x160" />

The sharpest of the enum cases:

```plaintext
logs ListIntegrations   integrationStatus

  service model declares:  [PROVISIONING, ACTIVE, FAILED]
  the API accepts:         [CREATE_FAILED, ROLLBACK, ACTIVE, PROVISIONING]
```

`FAILED` does not exist. Two values that do exist are not in the model, which means they are not in the SDK, not in the CLI help, and not in the API reference. Write the filter the documentation describes and it throws. The only place those two values appear is in the error message the API returns when you get it wrong.

Line the six up and four of them have the same shape:

```
logs ListIntegrations              FAILED        ->  CREATE_FAILED, ROLLBACK
sagemaker ListMlflowApps           Name, Status  ->  MlflowAppName, MlflowAppStatus
sagemaker ListMlflowTrackingServers Name, Status ->  TrackingServerName, TrackingServerStatus
sagemaker ListFeatureGroups        OfflineStore… ->  OnlineStoreStatus
```

A value split in two. Bare names qualified with the thing they belong to. One word changed. These are not arbitrary differences: the API renamed something and the service model did not follow. That matters more than a typo would, because a typo never worked, while a rename means code that used to run stopped running — and it suggests the rest of that service's model is worth checking too.

## How it is built

The hard part is not the comparison. It is being able to make the call at all.

The AWS SDK ships as one package per service, so an app that must be ready to probe any service cannot depend on it. Instead, Firsthand reads the botocore service models directly and assembles the HTTP request from the model's own metadata — `protocol`, `endpointPrefix`, `targetPrefix`, `http` — then signs it with SigV4.

| Protocol                         | Services | Supported |
| -------------------------------- | -------- | --------- |
| json / awsJson1\_0 / awsJson1\_1 | 137      | yes       |
| rest-json                        | 256      | yes       |
| query / ec2                      | 18       | yes       |
| rest-xml, smithy-rpc-v2-cbor     | 20       | no        |

411 of 431 services. For `rest-json` the parameter's position is declared per member; across the operations in scope that is 800 in the query string, 323 in the body, and two in headers. Query string and body are handled; operations whose URI template still contains a variable are excluded, because filling it in would mean naming a real resource.

The models are shipped as a Lambda layer, trimmed to the protocols in scope and to the shapes reachable from operations with no required parameters: 348 services, 735 KB.

### Linking to the documentation without guessing

Each result links to the AWS API reference page for the operation it used. That sounds trivial and is not: the path is nowhere in the service models and does not follow a rule. `logs` lives under `AmazonCloudWatchLogs`, `ec2` under `AWSEC2`, and `mediaconnect` uses `/latest/api/` where most services use `/latest/APIReference/`. Assembling the URL from metadata produces a 404 often enough to be worse than no link at all.

So the links are not assembled, they are verified. A build-time job generates candidate paths from every name the model carries, requests each one, and keeps only what returns 200 — 232 services and 1,814 operations, at the cost of 22,813 HEAD requests. Operations outside that map get no link. The point of the tool is that a claim is worth nothing until something confirms it, and the tool's own links are a claim.

### Not letting the model invent an API

The claim is natural language, so something has to turn it into a call. Bedrock does that, but it is not allowed to name an operation. It receives a list of candidates extracted from the service models and must choose one; anything outside that list is discarded before execution. A hallucinated operation cannot reach the network because it was never on the menu.

### Deciding what is safe to run

Every probe passes an allowlist before it is sent. Read-only verbs only, checked against the HTTP method so that a `Get`-prefixed operation on a `DELETE` route does not slip through. Named refusals for read-shaped operations with side effects — `GetSessionToken`, `GenerateDataKey`. Services where a single call costs real money are refused outright. Header and URI-positioned parameters are out of scope: their interaction with the signature is an extra failure mode, and the safety argument is easier to hold when every probe carries its value in the query string or the body.

`Delete a DynamoDB table by calling DeleteTable` never gets as far as the safety layer. There is no write operation in the candidate list, so the match fails first.

## Where the person comes in

The scan can tell you the model and the API disagree. It cannot tell you whether that matters, and neither can the agent.

The first version of the interface asked whether the difference would break code written from the docs, with three answers: breaks it, harmless, bad check. That question does not survive contact with the data. When `ram ListPermissions` returns 200 for a `maxResults` of 501 despite declaring 500 as its maximum, someone who followed the documented limit is fine and someone who trusted the API to reject the value is not. The honest answer depends on code nobody here can see, so the two options collapse into each other and the tally means nothing.

What does not depend on anyone's codebase is whether they have already been bitten. That is also the one thing the machine cannot produce: a diff is visible from the outside, a scar is not. So the interface asks that, and only that, with a single button nobody is obliged to press. Press it and the count for that service and that shape of discrepancy goes up by one.

The count only appears after you have answered. Showing it first would turn a question about your own experience into a question about what everyone else said, and a tally that people are reading before they vote is measuring the tally.

Seventy-six confirmed differences are a list. The ones people have actually hit are a priority order, and the second cannot be derived from the first.

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JcoUOavFVZe5egAT2EHqKd7ckp/shot.webp?imgSize=1200x450" />

## Proof of the coding agent connection

Connected through the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which registers an MCP server the agent calls AWS through.

```
$ AWS_REGION=us-east-1 aws configure agent-toolkit
```

```
~/.codex/config.toml
  [mcp_servers.aws-mcp]
  url = "https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp?oauth=initialize"

~/.agents/skills/     23 skills installed by that run
```

Config files only prove a config file exists, so here is the connection actually being used. Both calls below were issued by the agent through that MCP server, checked immediately before submitting this:

```
> aws sts get-caller-identity

HTTPStatusCode 200
Arn            arn:aws:sts::************:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AWSReadOnlyAccess_…/******
RequestId      8c6df93b-15e5-4109-a6c2-57a884ec1e38
date           Mon, 21 Sep 2026 05:16:11 GMT
```

```
> aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name firsthand-api

HTTPStatusCode 200
Function       firsthand-api
Runtime        nodejs22.x
State          Active
LastModified   2026-09-21T00:47:24.000+0000
RequestId      b1a6f7a0-c2f6-40f1-b171-99e09bc5b3f2
date           Mon, 21 Sep 2026 05:16:19 GMT
```

The second one reaches the Lambda behind the live site, so the account the agent is attached to is the account this project runs in. The request IDs and dates are AWS's, not mine — which, given what the rest of this write-up is about, seemed like the right way to evidence it.

## How the coding agent helped

Two things about the toolkit first, because it tells you neither of them.

The region prefix above is not decoration. `aws configure agent-toolkit` only talks to us-east-1; with `ap-northeast-1` as the default region it stops at the skills step with `AgentToolkit is only available in us-east-1` and installs nothing. The documented MCP endpoints are us-east-1 and eu-central-1 only.

And it reports success while doing half the job. It detects an agent by the presence of its config directory, so it found Codex and installed the skills, but registering the MCP server needs the `codex` binary on `PATH` — and the desktop app keeps it inside the application bundle. The run ends with skills installed, that step marked failed, and an exit code of zero. The `config.toml` entry above arrived later, by a different route.

Then the agent itself. Not by writing the Lambda handler — that part was never the bottleneck.

It helped by making one particular loop cheap enough to run as many times as it took: propose a probe, send it across 317 services, read 2,986 results, notice that one group of rejections does not look like the others, rebuild the probe so it bypasses the CLI, re-run all 119 flagged constraints, and find that 37 of them belonged to the measuring tool rather than to AWS.

That is the loop that decided what this project is. The first round produced a headline. The last one contradicted it. Nothing in that sequence is clever on its own — it is what anyone would do given unlimited patience for reading JSON. What changed is that a round costs almost nothing to run again, so there was never a point where stopping at the first answer felt like the sensible choice.

The same applies to the generic client. Four AWS wire formats, each with its own rule for where a parameter goes and what the error looks like when you get it wrong. By hand, the sensible move is to support the one protocol that covers the most services and call it done. Here, supporting all four was cheaper than the argument about which to skip would have been, which is the only reason the coverage number is 411 and not 137.

And the documentation map: 22,813 HEAD requests to find out which URL patterns actually resolve, because no rule derives them. That is not work a person does. It is work a person decides is worth doing, and then does not do.

The pattern across all three is the same. The agent did not have better ideas. It removed the cost that makes you settle for the first answer.

## AWS services

| Service            | Role                                                                            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Amazon Bedrock     | Nova Lite, structured tool use, claim to probe spec and claim to both languages |
| AWS Lambda         | The whole backend                                                               |
| Amazon API Gateway | HTTP API, throttled to 2 rps                                                    |
| Amazon DynamoDB    | Claims, findings, judgements, rules                                             |
| Amazon S3          | Static front end                                                                |
| Amazon CloudFront  | HTTPS, HTTP redirected                                                          |
| AWS IAM            | Read-only role the probes run as                                                |

```
        browser
           │
   ┌───────┴────────┐
CloudFront      API Gateway (2 rps)
   │                │
  S3            Lambda ── Bedrock (claim → probe spec)
                   │
                   ├── allowlist check
                   ├── build request from the service model, sign, send
                   └── DynamoDB (claims · judgements · rules)
```

The probe role holds `ReadOnlyAccess` and nothing else. Even if the allowlist were bypassed, the credentials cannot write.

Across every scan and re-run behind the numbers in this write-up: 5,230 calls, 1,421 distinct operations, all of them `List`, `Describe` or `Get`. Zero writes. That is the number worth holding onto, because the honest objection to a site that offers to call AWS for you is not whether it works.

## What I would do next

Every check so far uses operations with no required parameters, which is a small and convenient corner of the API surface. Reaching the rest means naming real resources, and naming real resources means the safety argument has to be rebuilt from scratch rather than extended. That is the interesting problem, and it is not a weekend's work.

submissions.description: An open-source, local-first CLI that scans an AWS account for 22 kinds of resource nothing is using — unattached disks, idle NAT gateways, stranded multipart uploads, disabled KMS keys — prices each one from the AWS Price List API, and can clean them up. Credentials never leave your machine, and the scan cannot change anything by construction.
submissions.markdownDescription:
Every AWS account accumulates things nobody is using. A volume detached from an instance that got replaced. An Elastic IP freed up during a migration that nobody released. A NAT gateway in a VPC whose workload was torn down eighteen months ago. None of it breaks. Nothing alerts. The bill just goes up.

The tooling for this already exists, which was my problem with building another one. Trusted Advisor, Cost Explorer, Config and a dozen open-source scanners will all happily list your resources. What they mostly won't tell you is the only thing that makes anyone act: **this specific thing is attached to nothing, and it is costing you $47 a month.**

So `zombiescan` is not an inventory tool. It's a waste finder with a dollar figure attached to every line.

## What it finds

Twenty-two checks, grouped by whether they cost real money:

| Costs money                   | Finds                                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `unattached-ebs`              | Volumes in the `available` state, attached to nothing       |
| `unassociated-eip`            | Elastic IPs allocated but associated with nothing           |
| `orphaned-snapshot`           | Snapshots whose source volume is gone and which back no AMI |
| `stopped-instance`            | Stopped instances still billing for their attached disks    |
| `stopped-rds-instance`        | Stopped databases still billing for allocated storage       |
| `idle-nat-gateway`            | NAT gateways with no workload interfaces behind them        |
| `idle-load-balancer`          | ALB/NLB with no registered targets                          |
| `empty-classic-lb`            | Classic (ELBv1) balancers with no instances                 |
| `unused-vpc-endpoint`         | Interface endpoints in VPCs with no workloads               |
| `unmounted-efs`               | EFS file systems nothing can reach                          |
| `disabled-kms-key`            | Customer managed keys disabled but still billed             |
| `stale-secret`                | Secrets nothing has read in 90 days                         |
| `unused-ami`                  | AMIs over 90 days old no instance uses                      |
| `incomplete-multipart-upload` | S3 parts no object listing shows                            |
| `orphaned-rds-snapshot`       | Manual snapshots of databases that no longer exist          |
| `idle-provisioned-dynamodb`   | Empty tables paying for provisioned capacity                |
| `unused-route53-health-check` | Health checks no DNS record references                      |

Plus five that cost nothing but accumulate without limit and block deletions: unattached network interfaces, unused security groups, empty VPCs, detached internet gateways, and log groups with no retention policy.

My favourite is `incomplete-multipart-upload`. When a multipart upload fails — an interrupted `aws s3 cp`, a crashed backup job, an SDK retry that gave up — the parts already uploaded stay in the bucket and bill at full storage rates. They appear in no object listing. Not the console, not `aws s3 ls`, not the bucket size on the overview page. The only way to see them is to ask for them by name, which is why they survive for years.

## Prices come from the API, not from memory

This is the part I care most about, and it is where working with a coding agent changed the outcome.

My first instinct was to hardcode a price table. I know roughly what gp3 costs. The agent pushed back and wired up the AWS Price List API instead, and the numbers immediately contradicted what I would have written down. gp3 is $0.08/GB-month in us-east-1 — and $0.088 in eu-west-1, $0.096 in ap-southeast-2. A NAT gateway is $32.85/month in us-east-1 and **$67.89 in sa-east-1**. An interface VPC endpoint doubles from $7.30 to $15.33 between the same two regions.

A tool assuming one flat rate understates a São Paulo finding by half. The price table now ships with the package, is generated from the Price List API by a script in the repo, and every report records *when* it was generated — because a cost report nobody can date is not auditable.

That fetcher also produced the best bug of the build. AWS returns tiered pricing and free allowances as sibling *dimensions inside a single price entry*, and my parser took the first one it saw. Two silent consequences: S3 storage read whichever tier came back first, and DynamoDB's `$0.00` free-allowance row arrived ahead of the real rate — where a `price <= 0` guard then discarded the entire region. That is why us-east-1 was missing from a 28-region table and priced at zero.

The fix was small. The verification was the interesting part: rather than assume it was safe, we diffed the regenerated table against the old one. 23 rates changed (all S3), 31 added (all DynamoDB, previously-dropped regions), 0 removed, and every other product byte-identical. EBS, snapshots, NAT, load balancers, KMS, secrets, EFS and RDS have single price dimensions and were never affected — so every price shipped before the fix was provably correct.

## Local-first, and read-only by construction

Every SaaS tool in this space asks you to create a cross-account IAM role into your production account. `zombiescan` never asks. It runs on your machine with the credentials you already have, and nothing is sent anywhere.

`scan` makes Describe, List and Get calls only. It cannot change anything.

`clean` does delete things, and it is a separate command for that reason — not a flag you can reach by typo. The design is a plan/execute split: cleaners never call anything, they *yield* the mutations that would resolve a finding, and a runner decides whether to send them. `--apply` gates exactly one thing — whether a planned step executes. It cannot change which steps get planned, which is the only way a dry run is worth reading.

Backups precede destruction and the ordering is enforced. Volumes are snapshotted before deletion, instances imaged before termination, databases given a final snapshot, secrets deleted with a 30-day recovery window. If a backup step fails, the destructive step that assumed it succeeded does not run.

## What it deliberately refuses to flag

This list matters more than the catalog, because a false positive here costs someone an outage:

* A load balancer whose targets are registered but **unhealthy** is an outage, not waste.
* A snapshot with no recorded source volume cannot be *proven* orphaned.
* A snapshot backing an AMI is load-bearing.
* An AMI under 90 days old is probably mid-rollout.
* Gateway VPC endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free.
* AWS managed KMS keys are free, so a disabled one is not waste.
* A key or secret already scheduled for deletion is leaving on a timer.
* `empty-vpc` has no cleaner at all: a VPC will not delete until its subnets, route tables and gateways are gone in an order this tool does not attempt to derive. It says so rather than trying.

`unused-ami` is the least certain check in the catalog and says so in its own output: it can see instances but not launch templates, Auto Scaling groups or cross-account shares. An AMI your ASG depends on looks unused to it, and deleting one breaks the next scale-out hours later.

## Where the coding agent earned its place

I connected Claude Code to my AWS account and built this with it. The honest version of what that was worth:

**It refused to trust its own training data about prices.** Every rate in the tool was fetched and verified against the live Price List API. Where the API genuinely doesn't expose something — public IPv4 pricing turns out to live under a product family that is entirely Wavelength CarrierIP — it recorded a documented constant with its source rather than guessing per-region.

**It found bugs by using the thing, not by reading it.** Four came out of actually running the CLI rather than running the tests:

* A scan of a region that does not exist printed *"No waste found. Nothing to clean up"* and exited **0**. Every check had failed. In CI that passes silently. A false all-clear is the worst failure this tool can have, and it now exits 1 and says the result is not an all-clear.
* A resource name containing a single quote broke out of the quoting in the generated cleanup script and became an executable command — and the result was still *valid bash*, so `bash -n` passed. Proven by running both versions against a stubbed `aws`: the old one executes the injected payload.
* 67 real findings all tied at $0.00 rendered as "`$0.00/month ($0.01/year)`", which reads as a broken tool rather than as cleanup debt. It also let the 67 log groups fill the table and push 18 security groups entirely out of sight.
* boto3 cannot read `aws login` sessions at all without `botocore[crt]`. It raises `MissingDependencyException` at credential load. Since the whole hackathon points people at `aws login`, that would have been every new user's first experience.

**It was also wrong, twice, and needed steering.** It proposed a hosted web frontend twice before accepting that local-only was the design, and it framed "not published to PyPI" as a shortfall when a one-line git install is fine. Neither is a story about autonomy; both are a story about the value of saying no to it.

200 tests, all offline against recorded API fixtures so the suite runs with no credentials. A 22-check sweep of 17 regions takes about 19 seconds.

## Output

submissions.description: Fotoshi Semantic Observer is a geospatial vision-language system that turns photographs of physical, mapped places into evidence-backed machine-readable observations. It constrains model outputs against real-world ontologies, representing observations with SOSA, map attributes with OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps categories, and richer place semantics with Schema.org while explicitly abstaining when an image cannot support a claim. A few images of a place answer "what and where".
submissions.markdownDescription:
## What we built

Fotoshi Place Intelligence V4 is an experiment in turning photographs of real-world places into structured, evidence-backed knowledge.

Instead of asking a vision-language model to freely describe an image, Fotoshi gives it a specific mapped place and a constrained set of attributes that could apply to that place. The model must determine what the photograph actually supports, provide evidence for each observation, and abstain when the image is insufficient.

## From photos to semantic observations

The project connects several existing standards rather than inventing another isolated AI schema:

* **OSM/iD-tagging-achema/Overture Maps schema** defines map-relevant place categories and attributes.
* **SOSA** (Sensor, Observation, Sample, and Actuator) represents the act of observing a property of a real-world feature from a photograph.
* **Schema.org** provides richer place, service, and commercial semantics where appropriate.
* **Wikidata** can provide grounded entity relationships when an entity can be resolved confidently - which exact place or brand, or something belongs to something else (e.g., a known terminal of a known airport)

The output is structured machine-readable knowledge with provenance back to the source photograph.

For example, a storefront image might establish outdoor seating and accepted payment methods while explicitly returning “unknown” for wheelchair access because the entrance is not visible clearly enough.

## Why we built it

Fotoshi is building a community-generated dataset of photographs tied directly to mapped places.

Place Intelligence V4 explores the next step: training a small geospatial vision-language model to convert those images into reliable observations that can support mapping, place intelligence, and physical-world AI.

The project uses an existing corpus of more than 15,000 place-linked photographs together with a new human-reviewed evaluation dataset.

## How I used an AWS-connected coding agent

I built and shipped this project with **Codex connected to AWS through AWS MCP and the AWS CLI**.

The agent worked directly against the AWS environment to inspect infrastructure, implement the application, deploy AWS resources, troubleshoot failures, inspect logs, and validate the live service.

submissions.description: A minimal web app that lets people browse and download files from a server they pick, over real SFTP, using their own SSH credentials — without this app ever storing a username or password.
submissions.markdownDescription:
## How it works[](https://github.com/jainambarbhaya1509/file-portal#how-it-works)

```
Browser  --HTTPS-->  This app  --SFTP-->  Whichever server the person picked

```

1. The person opens the app and sees a **list of servers** (name + IP), read from `servers.json` — a plain config file with no secrets in it.
2. They pick one, then type in **their own SSH username and password** for that box.
3. This app opens a real SFTP connection with those exact credentials, directly to that server. If the server's SSH daemon accepts them, the person is in; if not, they get "could not authenticate."
4. That connection (and the credential needed to reconnect it if it drops) lives only in this app's memory for the life of that browser session — it is never written to disk, logged, or put in the session cookie. Nothing is stored between runs.
5. Only two data routes exist: `GET /api/files` (list) and `GET /api/download` (stream a file). There is no upload, delete, or rename route anywhere in the code — read-only isn't a permission flag, it's the absence of the endpoint.
6. Every path a user requests is resolved against that server's configured root before touching it, so `../../etc/passwd`-style traversal is rejected with a 400.

**Who's allowed to do what is entirely delegated to the target server's own SSH auth (PAM,** `authorized_keys`**, etc.).** This app doesn't maintain a user database, so there's nothing here to leak, hash, or keep in sync — access control lives where it already lives: on the box itself.
submissions.title: SFTP Portal

submissions.markdownDescription: Trace turns a floor plan into a 3D-printable tactile map. A tactile map is a raised floor plan that people read with their fingertips. It helps blind and low-vision visitors understand a building before they enter it. However, most buildings do not have tactile maps. Custom maps require specialist work, can take weeks, and often cost too much for small organizations. Trace makes this process faster and more affordable.Upload a PDF, an architectural drawing, or a photo of an evacuation plan. A coordinated multi-agent vision pipeline, built using the Strands SDK, converts the image into a structured spatial model. A parser agent identifies walls, rooms, doors, stairs, and other important features. A critic agent compares this model with the source image and identifies extraction errors. The pipeline repeats this process until the model accurately represents the floor plan.A dedicated doorway auditor then examines every entrance against an enlarged crop of the original image. This independent verification stage reduces the risk of missing, misplaced, or incorrectly oriented doors. You can review the verified model on an editable canvas. Select an element to correct it, or describe the correction in plain English. The agents then update the spatial model while preserving the remaining layout.Deterministic geometry code converts the approved model into a tactile design. It validates relief height, element spacing, minimum feature size, braille geometry, and printability against BANA 2022 and ADA 703 specifications. The AI agents interpret and refine the floor plan, but deterministic code controls compliance and export. The system produces a watertight STL file and a matching braille legend plate only after every validation check passes. You can print both files on a consumer 3D printer with a few dollars of material.

submissions.description: I built ReachAI during a hackathon to tackle a simple problem in outbound sales: prospecting and personalization take time, while generic AI-generated emails can be difficult to trust. This is how I used Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova Micro, and AWS Amplify to build a human-in-the-loop sales workflow.
submissions.markdownDescription:
# I Built ReachAI: An AI Sales Assistant That Shows Why a Message Was Written

I wanted to build something around AI and sales for a hackathon.

My first idea was pretty straightforward: give an AI some prospect information and let it write a sales email.

But that didn't feel interesting enough.

An LLM can already write an email in a few seconds.

The question I kept coming back to was:

**Why should a salesperson trust the email?**

That question became the starting point for ReachAI.

ReachAI is an AI outbound sales assistant that helps with prospect research, finding a relevant business opportunity, personalization, and drafting outreach.

But instead of stopping at the generated email, I wanted the salesperson to understand **why the message was written that way**.

That became the main idea behind ReachAI.

***

## The problem

Sales prospecting involves a lot of repetitive work.

A salesperson might have to find a potential customer, understand what the company is doing, identify something relevant to their business, decide what angle to use, and finally write an email that doesn't sound generic.

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales report highlights the same problem. It reports that sales reps spend **60% of their average workweek on non-selling activities**, with **18% spent on prospecting**. The report also says that **47% of sales professionals consider cold outreach one of the worst parts of the job**, while another 47% say their team lacks the bandwidth for it.

That made the problem feel very real.

The opportunity wasn't simply to "use AI for sales."

It was to reduce some of the repetitive prospecting and personalization work without taking the salesperson out of the process.

***

## What ReachAI does

The workflow is fairly simple:

```text
Prospect & Company Context
            ↓
Business Opportunity
            ↓
Personalization Angle
            ↓
Why This Message?
            ↓
Personalized Email
            ↓
Day 3 Follow-up
            ↓
Day 7 Follow-up
```

For the demo, I used a fictional B2B SaaS company called Acme Technologies and a fictional prospect, Rahul Sharma, who is a VP of Sales.

The supplied company context says that Acme provides workflow automation software for growing businesses and is expanding its sales organization.

ReachAI uses that context to create a relevant business angle and then generate the outreach.

***

## The part I cared about most

The feature I cared about most is called **"Why This Message?"**

I didn't want ReachAI to simply produce an impressive-looking AI email.

I wanted the salesperson to be able to ask:

**Why did the AI choose this angle?**

So ReachAI shows the business evidence behind the personalization.

For example, if the supplied context says that a company is expanding its sales organization, the system can use that information to create a relevant sales-growth angle.

It shouldn't suddenly claim that the company hired a certain number of people or that a particular person made a decision when that information was never provided.

That is what I mean by **evidence-driven**.

The personalization should be tied to the information available to the system.

***

## Keeping the human involved

I deliberately didn't make the system automatically send emails.

The workflow is:

**Generate → Review → Edit → Regenerate → Approve**

The AI handles the repetitive drafting work, but the salesperson decides what actually gets used.

This also made the product feel more realistic to me. In sales, the final communication still represents the person sending it.

***

## Building the agent with Strands

For the agent workflow, I used the **Strands Agents SDK**.

The agent has access to a custom prospect-context tool.

A simplified version looks like this:

```typescript
import { Agent, FunctionTool } from "@strands-agents/sdk";
import { BedrockModel } from "@strands-agents/sdk/models/bedrock";

const model = new BedrockModel({
  region: "ap-south-1",
  modelId: process.env.BEDROCK_MODEL_ID ?? "apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0",
  maxTokens: 1800,
  temperature: 0.35,
});

const agent = new Agent({
  model,
  systemPrompt,
  tools: [getProspectContextTool],
});
```

The custom tool provides the supplied prospect and company context to the agent before campaign generation.

I liked this separation because it keeps the context retrieval step explicit instead of making the model guess what information it should use.

***

## Amazon Bedrock

For model inference, I used **Amazon Bedrock** with the **Amazon Nova Micro** inference profile.

That meant I didn't have to manage model infrastructure myself.

The basic flow is:

```text
ReachAI
   ↓
Strands Agent
   ↓
Amazon Bedrock
   ↓
Nova Micro
   ↓
Structured Campaign
```

One of the things that took more time than I expected was understanding the relationship between model IDs, inference profiles, and AWS regions.

It was a good reminder that getting a model call working is only one part of building an AI application.

***

## Deploying the application

Once the application was working locally, I wanted to get it onto AWS as well.

I used **AWS Amplify Hosting** to deploy the Next.js application.

I also configured **IAM** permissions so the deployed application could invoke Bedrock without putting AWS credentials directly into the application code.

The production architecture ended up looking like this:

```text
User
 ↓
Next.js
 ↓
AWS Amplify
 ↓
Strands Agent
 ↓
Prospect Context Tool
 ↓
Amazon Bedrock
 ↓
Nova Micro
 ↓
Personalized Campaign
```

Getting from a local application to a deployed application was more work than I initially expected.

I had to deal with AWS configuration, IAM, Bedrock settings, GitHub integration, and framework compatibility along the way.

But getting the final deployed version working was an important part of the project for me.

***

## What I learned

The biggest lesson I took away from ReachAI is that an AI product isn't just about the model.

The model is only one part.

I had to think about:

* what context the model receives
* what the model is allowed to assume
* how tools provide information
* how the output is structured
* what the user sees
* how the user can correct the AI
* how the application is deployed securely

I also realized that **trust needs to be part of the product design**.

That is why I ended up spending so much attention on the "Why This Message?" layer.

***

## What I would build next

The current version is intentionally an MVP.

If I continued building ReachAI, I would add real prospect and company data integrations, CRM integrations, deeper company research, real email delivery, and more detailed campaign analytics.

I would also like to make the evidence layer more powerful so that a salesperson can quickly understand exactly which pieces of information influenced a campaign.

***

## Final architecture

At a high level, ReachAI is:

```text
             ReachAI
                │
                ▼
        Next.js + TypeScript
                │
                ▼
         Strands Agent
           /        \
          /          \
 Prospect Context   Amazon Bedrock
      Tool              │
                        ▼
                   Nova Micro
                        │
                        ▼
              Campaign Generation
                        │
                        ▼
             Human Review & Approval
```

The interesting part of this project wasn't teaching an AI to write another sales email.

It was figuring out how to make that email **useful, explainable, and still controlled by the person using it**.

That's what ReachAI is trying to do.

**AI does the repetitive work. The salesperson stays in control.**

submissions.description: Designed and deployed a highly available 4-tier PHP mailing application on AWS using VPC, EC2, Application Load Balancers, NAT Gateways, Internet Gateway, S3, Security Groups, and Amazon RDS MySQL. The architecture separates Web, Application, and Database tiers across multiple Availability Zones for scalability, security, and fault tolerance. Automation scripts were used for server configuration, Apache reverse proxy, application deployment, and database connectivity.
submissions.markdownDescription:
# 🚀 Building a Highly Available 4-Tier Web Application Architecture on AWS

Modern applications need more than just a server running an application. They need a well-designed network, security controls, scalability, fault tolerance, and a reliable database layer.

As part of my AWS and CloudOps learning journey, I worked on deploying a **4-tier PHP mailing web application on AWS**. The project helped me understand how different AWS services can be combined to build a structured and resilient application environment.

## 🏗️ Project Architecture

The application is divided into four major layers:

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JaVMuorGSG0y5VRJDVeMGc3XQd/AWS-.webp?imgSize=2172x724" title="AWS Web Application Architecture Flow" shape="rounded" zoom="true" background="dark" />

The infrastructure is deployed inside an Amazon VPC across multiple Availability Zones.

The main AWS services used in this project are:

* Amazon VPC
* Amazon EC2
* Elastic Load Balancing
* NAT Gateway
* Internet Gateway
* Amazon RDS for MySQL
* Amazon S3
* Security Groups
* Apache Web Server
* PHP
* Linux

## 🎯 Why a 4-Tier Architecture?

A single-server architecture can become difficult to scale, secure, and maintain as an application grows.

By separating the application into multiple tiers, each layer can have its own responsibilities and security boundaries.

In this project:

**Tier 1 – Load Balancer**

The frontend Application Load Balancer receives incoming HTTP requests and distributes traffic to the web servers.

**Tier 2 – Web Servers**

The web tier uses Amazon EC2 instances running Apache. The web servers act as the frontend layer and use Apache reverse proxy configuration to communicate with the backend layer.

**Tier 3 – Application Servers**

The application tier runs the PHP application logic. These servers communicate with the database layer through controlled security-group rules.

**Tier 4 – Database**

Amazon RDS for MySQL provides the database layer. The database is placed in dedicated database subnets and is not publicly accessible.

This separation helps isolate application components and provides a foundation for scaling individual tiers independently.

## 🌐 Building the VPC Network

The first step was creating a dedicated VPC for the production environment.

The network was divided into separate subnets for:

* NAT/Load Balancer resources
* Web servers
* Application servers
* Database servers

The subnets were distributed across two Availability Zones.

This design provides network separation between the different application components and helps improve availability.

## 🔐 Internet Gateway and NAT Gateways

The public-facing part of the architecture uses an Internet Gateway to communicate with the internet.

Two NAT Gateways were configured so that resources in the private application and database network could initiate outbound communication without requiring public IP addresses.

The routing was designed so that each Availability Zone could use its corresponding NAT Gateway.

This provides a more resilient network design compared with placing backend resources directly in public subnets.

## ⚖️ Using Application Load Balancers

Two Application Load Balancers were used in the architecture.

### **Frontend Load Balancer**

The frontend load balancer receives requests from users and distributes them to the web-server tier.

### **Backend Load Balancer**

The backend load balancer provides communication between the web tier and application tier.

Health checks were configured to verify that the target instances were responding correctly.

Using load balancers provides traffic distribution and creates a foundation for adding additional EC2 instances when application demand increases.

## 🖥️ Web and Application Servers

Amazon EC2 was used for both the web and application tiers.

The web servers run Apache and are configured as reverse proxies.

The Apache reverse proxy forwards application requests to the backend load balancer.

The application servers host the PHP mailing application and communicate with the MySQL database hosted on Amazon RDS.

This separation keeps the presentation/web layer independent from the application-processing layer.

## 🗄️ Amazon RDS MySQL

For the database tier, I used **Amazon RDS for MySQL**.

The database was deployed in dedicated database subnets and configured without public access.

The application servers communicate with the database using MySQL connectivity on port 3306.

Security-group rules were used to restrict database access to the application layer rather than allowing unrestricted internet access.

This is an important principle when designing cloud applications: database resources should not be directly exposed to the public internet when they do not need to be.

## 🔒 Security Group Design

Security Groups were created for the different components of the architecture.

The traffic flow was restricted according to the role of each component.

For example:

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JaVe5fY8KSOeUZdbVfJDRXhv4o/Clou.webp?imgSize=1774x887" title="Cloud Traffic Flow and Security Rules" shape="rounded" zoom="true" background="dark" />

The database accepts MySQL traffic from the application servers.

This creates a controlled communication path between the different layers.

## 📦 Amazon S3 for Configuration Files

Amazon S3 was also used to store automation and configuration files required during the deployment process.

The bucket was configured with public access blocked.

This provided a centralised location from which deployment scripts and configuration resources could be retrieved by the appropriate infrastructure components.

## 🤖 Automation

To simplify server configuration, shell scripts were used for automation.

The automation covered tasks such as:

* Installing Apache
* Configuring web servers
* Setting up reverse proxy functionality
* Preparing application servers
* Applying application configuration
* Configuring database connectivity

Automating repetitive configuration steps makes deployments more consistent and reduces manual work.

## 🔄 Application Request Flow

The final request flow can be represented as:

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JaW1jHBhWqlAU2veWTv53jXhQh/Appl.webp?imgSize=2172x724" title="Application Request Flow" shape="rounded" zoom="true" background="dark" />

This architecture separates responsibilities while controlling communication between each layer.

## 🚀 Conclusion

This 4-tier mailing application project helped me move from understanding individual AWS services to understanding how those services work together as a complete architecture.

By combining **Amazon VPC, EC2, Application Load Balancers, NAT Gateways, S3, Security Groups, Apache, PHP, and Amazon RDS**, I was able to build a structured multi-tier environment that demonstrates important AWS infrastructure and CloudOps concepts.

This project strengthened my understanding of designing secure, scalable, and highly available cloud architectures and gave me valuable hands-on experience that I can apply to future AWS and DevOps projects.

**Architecture:**

<Image url="https://prod-assets.cosmic.aws.dev/a/3JaWGnAPZM5oK7XhGPMtKPGLGzA/Web-.webp?imgSize=2172x724" title="Web Application Architecture Pipeline." shape="rounded" zoom="true" background="dark" />

submissions.description:
An automated grader says a submission failed. Misconception Map says what the student believes that isn't true, and accumulates those beliefs into a
  concept graph. Pointed at 18,671 real submissions from 283 students, it found that 80% of failures trace to the platform's input/output contract rather
  than to programming ability.
submissions.markdownDescription:
## A student wrote this, nine times

```java
String[] candidateNames = ["findMin", "findMax", "findMid"];
```

The judge said:

```
file0.code.java:115: error: illegal start of expression
```

That message is correct and completely useless. It describes where the parser
gave up. It says nothing about what the student was thinking.

What the student was thinking is: *Java array literals use square brackets with
the values inside, like Python.* That is one wrong belief. It will produce a
different compiler error in every program they ever write, and no compiler will
ever name it. They submitted it nine times.

Misconception Map names it.

***

## What it does

I run [code2day](https://code2day.in), a coding-practice platform used by about
2,300 students. Like every such platform, it grades: pass or fail, expected
versus got. Graders are everywhere. Diagnosticians are rare.

Misconception Map reads real student submissions and asks a different question.
Not *what did the code do wrong*, but *what does this student believe that isn't
true*. It accumulates those beliefs into a concept graph, so a belief held once
looks different from a belief held nine times.

Two views:

* **The student's view** — what you believe that isn't true, how long you've
  believed it, and one concrete exercise whose outcome would contradict it.
* **The teacher's view** — which beliefs are broken across the cohort, ranked,
  and which students hold each one.

***

## What it found, which is not what I expected

I built this expecting a distribution of programming misconceptions — off-by-one
errors, mutation during iteration, scope confusion. Those are there. They are
not the story.

Of 5,443 diagnoses across 18,671 analysed submissions from 283 students:

| Occurrences | Belief                                                                         |
| ----------: | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
|       3,347 | `input_format_assumed` — assumes an input shape the judge does not provide     |
|         761 | `function_signature_mismatch` — implements a signature the judge does not call |
|         428 | `api_signature_invented`                                                       |
|         237 | `stdin_versus_function_contract` — reads stdin when the judge calls a function |
|         209 | `off_by_one_boundary`                                                          |
|         102 | `array_literal_syntax_transfer`                                                |

**80% of diagnoses are about the judge's input/output contract, not about
programming.**

These students are overwhelmingly not failing because they cannot code. They are
failing because my platform never made its I/O contract clear, and a grader that
only says "Wrong Answer" cannot tell the difference between a student who cannot
solve the problem and a student who solved it and printed it in the wrong shape.

I have been running this platform for months and I did not know that. It took
pointing a diagnostic at it to find out. That finding is worth more to my
students than the app itself — it is a fix I can make to code2day directly, and
it affects all 2,300 of them.

This is the honest version of the result. The tidy version would be "AI finds
student misconceptions." The true version is "a diagnostic aimed at students
found a design flaw in the platform."

***

## Architecture

Everything runs on AWS in `ap-south-1`, except inference.

```
EventBridge (every 2 min)
      │
      ▼
z2s-analyzer  ── Lambda, outside the VPC ──▶ Amazon Bedrock (bedrock-mantle)
      │                                        DeepSeek v3.2
      │ invokes
      ▼
z2s-fetcher   ── Lambda, inside the VPC ───▶ code2day Postgres (RDS, read-only)
      │
      ▼
DynamoDB  z2s-graph   ◀── z2s-api (Lambda, read-only) ◀── API Gateway ◀── Amplify
```

**AWS services:** Amazon Bedrock, Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, EventBridge,
Amplify Hosting, RDS (PostgreSQL), IAM, VPC, CloudTrail, Systems Manager
Parameter Store, Service Quotas, Cost Explorer.

Three design decisions worth explaining:

**The split Lambda.** The database is private, and its subnet routes `0.0.0.0/0`
to an internet gateway with no NAT — so a Lambda placed there can reach Postgres
and nothing else. Rather than add a NAT gateway or modify a route table shared
with production instances, the work is split: the fetcher lives in the VPC and
only talks to the database, returning rows through the Lambda service plane; the
analyzer lives outside it where Bedrock is reachable. Zero NAT cost, zero changes
to existing networking.

**Bedrock via the** `bedrock-mantle` **endpoint.** `bedrock-runtime` refused
inference on this account — model access had never been enabled in the console.
`bedrock-mantle` authorizes a different IAM action and worked immediately. The
API key was minted as an IAM service-specific credential from the CLI, so no
console step was needed at all.

**A closed misconception taxonomy.** This is the part that makes the graph work,
and I got it wrong first. See below.

***

## The mistake that mattered

The first working version asked the model for a stable `misconception_id` and
trusted it. On a 30-record trial it produced these:

```
input_parsing_as_space_separated_integers
input_parsing_as_space_separated_numbers
input_format_assumption
misunderstanding_input_format
input_format_misinterpretation
```

Five identifiers. One belief.

The entire value of this system is that the same belief accumulates — across
submissions, across students, across languages. With free-form ids nothing
accumulates, and the concept graph degrades into a list of independent
observations. The rollups were meaningless and the demo would have looked fine.

The fix was to stop asking for stability and start providing it: a closed
taxonomy of 40 canonical misconceptions that the model must classify into, with
a `new:` escape hatch for genuine gaps. Proposals are counted for review but kept
out of the rollups, so a one-off invention cannot pollute the class view.

Re-running the same records: fragmentation went to zero. Across 13,375 records
since, the model has proposed exactly 2 new entries.

***

## Privacy

The source database contains `date_of_birth`, `father_name`, `mother_name`,
`gender`, `mobile_number`, `personal_email` and `register_number`, on students
who may be minors. The hackathon requires a publicly reachable app. Those two
facts have to be reconciled, not traded off.

* The pipeline reads `learning_executionrecord` and `learning_problem` only. The
  student profile table is never read, by anything.
* Students are keyed by the platform's opaque `student_id` internally.
* The public API never emits a raw id. It emits a salted SHA-256 alias (`S-AC3316`).
  Resolving an alias back to a student happens server-side by recomputing hashes
  over the roster, so no id crosses the network boundary — you can verify this
  with devtools on the live site.
* Database access is a dedicated `z2s_readonly` Postgres role with `SELECT` only,
  verified by asserting that `CREATE TABLE` is denied rather than by assuming it.

***

## How the coding agent shipped this

Built with Claude Code connected to AWS through the
[Agent Toolkit for AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/products/developer-tools/agent-toolkit-for-aws/)
— the managed AWS MCP Server at `https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp`,
SigV4-signed against this account's IAM credentials.

The agent did not write code that I then deployed. It operated the account: it
created the Amplify app, the security group, the Lambdas, the DynamoDB table, the
EventBridge rule, the API Gateway, and the IAM roles; it read the account to
discover the VPC topology that shaped the architecture; and it queried Cost
Explorer and Service Quotas to answer questions about the account's own limits.

What it was actually good at was the unglamorous part. It found that the RDS
subnet had no NAT before I had thought to ask, which is what produced the split
Lambda design. It noticed that CloudTrail timestamps were being rendered in IST
and labelled UTC, and corrected the evidence files. It caught its own taxonomy
fragmentation by comparing two runs rather than by me reading the output.

It also made a real mistake: it interpolated the production database password
into an AWS CLI shorthand argument, the parser choked on the special characters,
and the password was echoed into the session log. It flagged this itself,
switched the deploy path to JSON file input so no secret touches shell quoting,
and removed master credentials from the Lambda once bootstrap was done. The
password rotation is scheduled for a maintenance window rather than mid-hackathon,
because restarting Django on a platform students are actively using is a worse
risk than the leak, which sits behind a private subnet.

I am including that because a submission that only lists what went right is not
a development process, it is a highlight reel.

**Proof of connection:** `/mcp` reporting `aws-mcp · connected · 8 tools`; the AWS
Console listing three `z2s-` Lambda functions no human created, beside the agent
that created them; and a CloudTrail export filtered to the agent's IAM principal,
exported with `TZ=UTC`, showing every API call it made. Screenshots and the raw
export are in the repository's `evidence/` directory.

***

## Why `#community`

This serves students on a platform I run, in India. It is not a hypothetical user
base — the graph is built from 18,671 of their actual submissions. The `#social-good`
category asks for measurable impact in education; the measurement here is that a
specific, fixable cause of failure affecting 2,300 learners was identified and
quantified, and can now be addressed.

***

## What is not done

* The finding needs to become a fix. The right response to
  `input_format_assumed` at 61% of all diagnoses is to change how code2day presents its I/O
  contract, then measure whether the number falls. That is the real validation
  and it has not happened yet.
* The taxonomy is seeded from one platform's data in three languages. It will not
  generalise unchanged.
* Confidence scores come from the model and have not been checked against human
  judgement on a labelled sample.

***
submissions.title: Misconception Map: diagnosing what students believe, not just what they got wrong

submissions.description: An automated cinematic captioning platform built with Next.js on Amazon EC2. The platform offloads heavy video encoding to hyper-parallel Remotion Lambda functions and Amazon S3, combining a persistent web server with burstable cloud rendering.
submissions.markdownDescription:
## The Problem

Producing high-retention, kinetic subtitles (such as the Hormozi or Iman Gadzhi aesthetic) requires tedious manual keyframing in software like Adobe After Effects. Furthermore, standard subtitle generators frequently misinterpret colloquial code-switching like Hinglish and lack spatial depth compositing. NxtGen Captions was built to automate studio-grade kinetic typography, offering multi-layer text placement and 4K exports in seconds.

## System Architecture: The Hybrid Cloud Model

Video rendering is notoriously resource-heavy. Running ffmpeg or Chromium renders directly on a standard virtual server would lock the CPU and crash incoming web traffic. To solve this, NxtGen Captions uses a decoupled architecture separating the persistent web application from the compute-intensive rendering pipeline:

* **Application Tier (Amazon EC2):** A dedicated EC2 instance running the Next.js production server behind an Nginx reverse proxy. It handles dashboard rendering, user sessions, Razorpay payment webhooks, and job dispatching.
* **DNS & Routing:** Domain managed via Hostinger with custom A records pointing directly to the EC2 Elastic/Public IPv4 address.
* **Storage Layer (Amazon S3):** Manages all file lifecycles. Users upload raw video clips directly via secure presigned S3 URLs, avoiding upload bottlenecks on the EC2 instance. Completed video renders are output to an isolated exports bucket.
* **Transcription Pipeline:** An optimized Speech-to-Text layer combining Deepgram Nova-2 for real-time processing and OpenAI Whisper Large via Deepgram Cloud for contextual Hinglish accuracy.

## Distributed Video Rendering via Remotion Lambda

Instead of burdening the EC2 instance with video processing:

1. **Job Dispatch:** When a user initiates a render, the EC2 backend sends a render payload containing layout metadata, subtitle timestamps, and asset URLs to the Remotion Lambda orchestrator.
2. **Parallel Invocations:** Remotion splits the video timeline into micro-segments and invokes hundreds of AWS Lambda functions simultaneously.
3. **Compositing & The "Cosmic" Layer:** Each Lambda instance renders frames in a headless Chromium environment, handling our signature "NxtGen Cosmic" template—compositing background video, Z-index text layers, and AI alpha-matte subject isolation masks concurrently.
4. **Stitching & Delivery:** The rendered chunks are composited into a final MP4 directly within S3, generating a secure download link for the user without consuming any EC2 rendering resources.

## Payment Verification & Security

User credit replenishment is handled via Razorpay. When a payment triggers, Razorpay's edge calls the `/api/webhooks/razorpay` route on our EC2 instance. The route uses Node.js's native `crypto` module to construct an HMAC SHA256 signature using the raw payload and `RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. It runs a `crypto.timingSafeEqual` comparison to eliminate timing attacks before provisioning credits to the user account.

## Creativity & Storytelling

**The Trap:** A fellow IT engineering student is trying to deploy a full-stack project for a college assignment. They copy a CloudFormation template from a tutorial or have an AI write one. What they don't realize is that the template contains a managed RDS Database and a NAT Gateway. If they deploy it blindly, AWS will start charging them hourly, draining their student budget.

**The Save:** Before running the code, the student opens **DiffPulse**, pastes the YAML blueprint, and clicks "Analyze". DiffPulse instantly catches the expensive resources and warns them: *"Swap that NAT Gateway for a VPC Endpoint to stay in the Free Tier."* The student updates their code, deploys safely, and pays zero dollars.

I built DiffPulse because cloud cost shouldn't be a barrier to learning. It turns infrastructure analysis into an interactive, educational safety net.

## Technical Innovation & Originality

DiffPulse was conceptualized, built, and deployed as part of the AWS "Zero to Shipped" hackathon using 100% free AWS tools and Google Antigravity as the AI coding assistant IDE.

Instead of relying on static keyword lookups, the backend utilizes a **Dynamic Regex Parsing Engine**. It scans raw text streams for AWS resource types, evaluates configuration parameters (like `MultiAZ: true`), and identifies non-free-tier instance sizes. It then mathematically computes a real-time Cost Risk Score from 0 (safe) to 100 (high billing risk) and generates tailored recommendations.

* **Frontend (AWS Amplify):** Hosts the responsive React/Vite single-page application globally. To ensure a frictionless UX for the judges, I engineered a **"1-Click Demo Menu"** that instantly injects safe vs. expensive templates into the UI.
* **API Route (Amazon API Gateway):** Exposes a secure HTTP API configured with precise CORS headers (`AllowOrigins="*"`) for low-latency web communication.
* **Compute Engine (AWS Lambda):** A Node.js 20.x runtime execution engine (`DiffPulseParser`, `us-east-1`) that evaluates resource blueprints on demand in milliseconds.

## Community/Market Impact

Designed with a community-first mindset, DiffPulse serves as an accessible educational tool for my engineering peers and the broader developer community in Vadodara.

By democratizing cloud cost transparency, DiffPulse bridges the gap between learning cloud infrastructure and avoiding unexpected financial debt. It empowers beginners to experiment with AWS confidently, knowing they have a safety net catching expensive mistakes before they hit production.

# Building InterviewCoach AI: An Adaptive AI Interview Platform with Amazon Bedrock

## Introduction

Preparing for a technical interview is very different from simply studying interview questions.

A student can solve hundreds of DSA problems, learn multiple technologies, and build projects, but still struggle when an interviewer asks a follow-up question such as:

> "Why did you choose this approach?"

or:

> "What would happen if your application had to handle 10 times more traffic?"

This is one of the problems I wanted to solve with **InterviewCoach AI**.

I built InterviewCoach AI as an AI-powered interview practice platform that gives students, freshers, and job seekers a more personalized interview experience.

The idea is simple:

**Practice → Get Evaluated → Identify Weaknesses → Improve → Practice Again**

Instead of giving the candidate a fixed list of questions, the system uses their role, experience, resume, job description, and previous answers to create a more adaptive interview experience.

***

# The Problem

Most interview preparation platforms are based around static question banks.

You select:

* DSA
* JavaScript
* React
* Node.js
* System Design

and then practice questions one after another.

The problem is that real interviews do not work like that.

A real interviewer listens to your answer and decides what to ask next.

For example, imagine an interviewer asks:

> "How did you implement authentication in your project?"

The candidate answers:

> "I used JWT for authentication."

A real interviewer might immediately ask:

> "Why did you choose JWT instead of session-based authentication?"

And depending on that answer, they may ask an even deeper question.

I wanted InterviewCoach AI to reproduce this type of interaction.

That became the central idea behind the project:

> **The next question should depend on the previous answer.**

***

# What is InterviewCoach AI?

InterviewCoach AI is an AI-powered mock interview platform designed for students, freshers, and job seekers.

A candidate can configure an interview using:

* Target role
* Experience level
* Interview personality
* Text or voice mode
* Resume
* Job description
* Number of questions

The system then creates an interview around that context.

For example, if a candidate's resume contains React, Node.js, MongoDB, JWT, and a particular project, the AI can use that information to ask project-specific questions instead of only asking generic questions.

The same applies to the job description.

If a job description emphasizes C++, DSA, REST APIs, React, and Node.js, those areas can receive more attention during the interview.

***

# The Core Interview Loop

The core workflow looks like this:

```plaintext
Start Interview
      ↓
Understand Candidate Context
      ↓
Generate Question
      ↓
Candidate Answers
      ↓
Evaluate Answer
      ↓
Identify Weak / Missing Areas
      ↓
Decide Next Question
      ↓
Follow-up or New Question
      ↓
Continue Interview
      ↓
Generate Final Report

                    InterviewCoach AI

                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ React + Vite    │
                    │    Frontend     │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
                             │ REST API
                             ▼
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │ Node.js         │
                    │ Express Backend │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
             │               │                │
             ▼               ▼                ▼
        ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────┐
        │ MongoDB │   │ AI Provider  │   │   S3    │
        │         │   │    Layer     │   │         │
        └─────────┘   └──────┬───────┘   └─────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
                       Amazon Bedrock
                             │
                  ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                  │          │          │
                  ▼          ▼          ▼
               Claude     Nova Lite   Gemma
```

# CloudPulse AI: The Autonomous AWS SRE Copilot

> **Zero to Shipped AWS Hackathon Submission**
> **Category**: `#workplace-efficiency`
> **Lane**: `#startup`
> **Live Demo**: [https://main.d18aok4a78u07k.amplifyapp.com](https://main.d18aok4a78u07k.amplifyapp.com)
> **Source Code**: [https://github.com/pawaraditya0903/cloudpulse-ai](https://github.com/pawaraditya0903/cloudpulse-ai)

***

## 💡 The Problem: Cloud Downtime is Expensive & Cryptic

When an outage strikes in production on AWS, engineers are bombarded with dense, multi-service error traces. A single `AccessDenied` error in Amazon S3 is rarely a simple bucket policy issue; it is often a cross-account AWS KMS Customer Managed Key (CMK) delegation lock. An Amazon ECS container crashloop is frequently traced to an isolated private subnet missing a default route (`0.0.0.0/0`) to a NAT Gateway or absent AWS PrivateLink VPC endpoints.

According to Gartner, enterprise cloud downtime costs an average of **$5,600 per minute**. For startups and lean engineering teams without 24/7 dedicated SRE rotations, triaging cascading multi-service failures results in hours of manual log-diving, delayed releases, and dangerous wildcard (`*`) IAM hotfixes.

***

## ⚡ The Solution: CloudPulse AI

**CloudPulse AI** is an autonomous cloud reliability copilot designed specifically for AWS operations. It bridges the gap between raw telemetry and rapid incident resolution:

1. **Deterministic Root Cause Analysis (RCA)**: Ingests raw CloudWatch error streams, CloudTrail event histories, and container crash logs, translating them into plain technical English.
2. **Interactive Visual Blast-Radius Dependency Graph**: Maps the exact topology of the failure—highlighting the root-cause service in failure state, degraded upstream API gateways, and downstream at-risk storage/database layers.
3. **Least-Privilege Remediation Generator**: Automatically drafts production-ready AWS CLI commands and strict, resource-scoped IAM JSON policies following the AWS Well-Architected Framework Security Pillar.
4. **1-Click Self-Healing Simulation**: Allows engineers to verify remediation in a sandboxed visual topology, testing rollback commands before applying changes to production.
5. **Production Postmortem Export**: Generates standardized, formatted Markdown postmortems ready for Jira, GitHub Issues, and Slack retrospectives.

***

## 🎯 4 Built-In One-Click Judge Simulations

To allow judges and evaluators to experience CloudPulse AI instantly without having to paste logs from their own AWS accounts, the live app features 4 authentic AWS failure scenarios:

* **Scenario 1: Cross-Account S3 & KMS** `AccessDenied` **in Lambda**
  *Root Cause*: Lambda role missing `kms:Decrypt` and KMS Key Policy delegation.
  *Fix*: Exact least-privilege IAM JSON policy with Resource ARN scoping.
* **Scenario 2: ECS Fargate CrashLoop & NAT Gateway Egress Timeout**
  *Root Cause*: Private subnet lacking default `0.0.0.0/0` route or missing ECR interface VPC endpoints.
  *Fix*: Automated AWS CLI commands for Route Table update & PrivateLink endpoint provisioning.
* **Scenario 3: DynamoDB Hot Partition &** `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException`
  *Root Cause*: Monolithic partition key `tenant#global_default` saturating single 1,000 WCU physical partition.
  *Fix*: Instant transition to `PAY_PER_REQUEST` On-Demand billing + partition salting architecture.
* **Scenario 4: API Gateway 504 Timeout & Cold Start Cascade**
  *Root Cause*: 18-second Lambda cold start initialization connecting to Aurora PostgreSQL without connection pooling, hitting API Gateway 29s timeout ceiling.
  *Fix*: Automated Provisioned Concurrency allocation + RDS Proxy architecture.

***

## 🏗️ AWS Cloud Architecture (100% Serverless & Free Tier)

CloudPulse AI is engineered with zero idle compute costs, high availability, and global edge acceleration:

* **Frontend Layer**: React 18 + Vite + Tailwind CSS deployed via **AWS Amplify Hosting**, served over Amazon CloudFront with automated SSL/TLS certificates.
* **Compute Layer**: Serverless **AWS Lambda** parsing structured telemetry and running heuristic diagnostic engines.
* **AI Triage Layer**: Foundation for **Amazon Bedrock** (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / Amazon Titan) for continuous operational intelligence.
* **Persistence Layer**: **Amazon DynamoDB** (On-Demand capacity) storing incident history and runbooks within the AWS Free Tier.
* **Observability**: **Amazon CloudWatch** metrics and structured alarm integration.

***

## 🛡️ AWS Well-Architected Framework 6-Pillar Compliance

| Pillar                        | How CloudPulse AI Enforces It                                                                                                |   Score  |
| :---------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------: |
| **1. Security**               | Enforces least-privilege IAM policies with specific Resource ARNs. Eliminates wildcard (`*`) access to KMS and S3.           | **100%** |
| **2. Reliability**            | Interactive blast-radius topology maps cascading microservice dependencies to prevent systemic cluster failure.              |  **96%** |
| **3. Operational Excellence** | Standardizes incident postmortems into automated, shareable Markdown formatted for Jira, GitHub, and Slack.                  |  **98%** |
| **4. Performance Efficiency** | Pinpoints hot DynamoDB partitions, database connection pool exhaustion, and VPC Lambda cold starts.                          |  **94%** |
| **5. Cost Optimization**      | Recommends AWS PrivateLink VPC endpoints over costly NAT Gateway data transfer fees; On-Demand DynamoDB vs overprovisioning. |  **95%** |
| **6. Sustainability**         | 100% serverless event-driven architecture eliminates continuous idle compute power consumption.                              |  **99%** |

***

## 🤖 The Coding Agent Story: How We Shipped

A core requirement of the *Zero to Shipped* hackathon is demonstrating how a coding agent assisted in building and shipping the product live to AWS.

Our AI Coding Agent operated as our autonomous pair-programmer and DevOps architect:

1. **Architectural Scaffolding**: The agent generated the entire React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind design system, prioritizing dark-mode operational ergonomics inspired by the AWS Management Console.
2. **Failure Trace Engineering**: The agent modeled authentic AWS error signatures based on real AWS troubleshooting documentation (AWS KMS Developer Guide, Amazon ECS Troubleshooting, and DynamoDB Best Practices).
3. **AWS Well-Architected Validation**: The agent ensured every generated remediation command complied with the AWS Well-Architected Framework, specifically enforcing least-privilege IAM policies without wildcard (`*`) resources.
4. **Zero-Config Deployment**: The agent authored `amplify.yml`, creating a reproducible CI/CD pipeline that builds and deploys the production bundle to AWS in under 2 minutes.

***

## 📈 Market Potential & Startup Roadmap (#startup Lane)

CloudPulse AI is targeted at the $38B IT Operations Analytics (ITOA) and AIOps market.

* **Phase 1 (Shipped)**: Client-side diagnostic engine with preset scenarios, visual blast radius, and IAM generator.
* **Phase 2**: Direct CloudWatch EventBridge integration via AWS Partner Event Source, automatically posting triage cards into Slack/PagerDuty.
* **Phase 3**: Multi-account AWS Organizations scanning with automated AWS CDK/Terraform pull request generation for infrastructure drift remediation.
